title: Mock exam 3
blurb: Drills the spots past papers keep reusing: invariants on pictures, captured bindings, and GUI "what does this edit break" questions.

items.prompt: True or false? (a) In Java, a variable of type int[] can hold null. (b) In OCaml, a variable of type int option can hold null. (c) In the OCaml ASM, a tail-recursive function processing a million-element list uses a constant number of stack slots. (d) In Java, == on two int values compares their numeric values.
items.key: (a) True; (b) False; (c) True; (d) True
items.notes: (b): OCaml has no null; None is an ordinary value of the option type. (d): == compares references only for objects; for primitives it compares values.

items.prompt: Is this function tail recursive?
items.code:
let rec find (p : 'a -> bool) (l : 'a list) : 'a option =
  begin match l with
  | [] -> None
  | x :: tl -> if p x then Some x else find p tl
  end
items.key: Tail recursive

items.prompt: Is this function tail recursive?
items.code:
let rec all_pos (l : int list) : bool =
  begin match l with
  | [] -> true
  | x :: tl -> all_pos tl && x > 0
  end
items.key: Not tail recursive
items.notes: Compare 25sp 1.5: the recursive call is the left operand of &&, so x > 0 must still be checked after it returns. Swapping the operands would make it tail recursive.

items.prompt: Is this function tail recursive?
items.code:
let rec count (q : 'a qnode option) (n : int) : int =
  begin match q with
  | None -> n
  | Some qn ->
    begin match qn.next with
    | None -> n + 1
    | Some _ -> count qn.next (n + 1)
    end
  end
items.key: Tail recursive
items.notes: n + 1 in the inner None arm is not a recursive call, so it does not matter. The only recursive call is the whole Some _ arm.

items.prompt: Is this function tail recursive?
items.key: Not tail recursive
items.notes: Having an accumulator is not enough. The + 0 is still work done after the call returns. Checked: it overflows a small stack on n = 1,000,000.

items.prompt: For each queue picture, name the broken invariant ((1), (2a) or (2b)), or say Valid. (i) q.head = Some n1, q.tail = None, n1.next = None. (ii) q.head = Some n1, q.tail = Some n2, n1.next = None, n2.next = None. (iii) q.head = Some n1, q.tail = Some n1, n1.next = Some n2, n2.next = None. (iv) q.head = None, q.tail = None, and some node m with m.next = Some m exists elsewhere in the heap. Queue invariant: (1) head and tail are both None or both Some; (2) if head = Some h and tail = Some t, then (2a) t is reachable from h by following next pointers and (2b) t.next = None.
items.key: (i) (1); (ii) (2a); (iii) (2b); (iv) Valid
items.notes: (iii): t = h, so (2a) holds trivially, but the tail's next is not None. (iv): the invariant only talks about nodes reachable from q; garbage elsewhere in the heap doesn't matter.

items.prompt: This deq is buggy. Give a valid input queue on which it breaks an invariant, say which invariant, and describe the queue afterwards.
items.key: Any one-element queue, such as [7]. After deq, q.head = None but q.tail = Some n (the removed node), which breaks (1). Queues with two or more elements stay valid.

items.prompt: Fix the deq from 2.2 by adding one line.
items.key:
After q.head <- n.next; add
  if n.next = None then q.tail <- None;
items.notes: Matching on n.next (| None -> q.tail <- None | Some _ -> ()) is also fine.

items.prompt: Write insert_after q x y: insert a new node with value y right after the first node whose value is x. If no node has value x, do nothing. The queue must stay valid; in particular, if x is in the last node, the new node becomes the tail. Must be tail recursive. Examples: [1; 2; 3] with x = 2, y = 9 gives [1; 2; 9; 3]; with x = 3 it gives [1; 2; 3; 9]; [1; 1] with x = 1 gives [1; 9; 1].
items.key:
let insert_after (q : 'a queue) (x : 'a) (y : 'a) : unit =
  let rec loop (no : 'a qnode option) : unit =
    begin match no with
    | None -> ()
    | Some n ->
      if n.v = x then begin
        let fresh = { v = y; next = n.next } in
        n.next <- Some fresh;
        if fresh.next = None then q.tail <- Some fresh
      end else loop n.next
    end
  in loop q.head
items.notes: Rubric idea: 4 pts traversal with stop at the first match, 4 pts build the node with next = n.next, 3 pts relink n.next, 3 pts update the tail when inserting at the end, 2 pts tail recursion. Writing n.next <- Some {v = y; next = None} loses the rest of the queue.

items.prompt: What is the value of r?
items.code:
let x = 10
let f (y : int) : int = x + y
let x = 100
let g = fun (z : int) -> f z + x
let r = g 1
items.key: 111  (f saved x = 10 when it was defined, so f 1 = 11; g reads the newer x = 100)
items.notes: The second let x makes a new binding; it does not change the old one. Closures keep the binding that was in scope when they were created.

items.prompt: Same code as 3.1. Which bindings are saved in f's closure? Choose all that apply: the first x (= 10), the second x (= 100), y, f, g.
items.key: Only the first x (= 10)
items.notes: y is f's parameter. The second x doesn't exist yet when f is defined.

items.prompt: Fill in the blanks in like_widget: a "Like" button next to a label that starts at "0 likes" and shows the running count ("1 likes", "2 likes", ...) after each click. Keep the count in a local mutable record.
items.code:
1 let like_widget () : widget =
2   let count = ____ in
3   let count_w, count_lc = label "0 likes" in
4   let btn_w, _, btn_nc = button "Like" in
5   let like () : unit =
6     ____;
7     ____ in
8   ____ (mouseclick_listener ____);
9   hpair (border btn_w) count_w
items.key:
1 let like_widget () : widget =
2   let count = { contents = 0 } in
3   let count_w, count_lc = label "0 likes" in
4   let btn_w, _, btn_nc = button "Like" in
5   let like () : unit =
6     count.contents <- count.contents + 1;
7     count_lc.set_label (string_of_int count.contents ^ " likes") in
8   btn_nc.add_event_listener (mouseclick_listener like);
9   hpair (border btn_w) count_w
items.notes: Questions 4.2 to 4.7 refer to this completed code by line number.

items.prompt: For each snippet, say what happens: what it prints, which exception it throws, or that it does not compile. (a) int[][] a = {{1, 2}, {3}}; System.out.println(a[1][1]); (b) int[][] a = new int[2][3]; a[0] = a[1]; a[0][0] = 7; System.out.println(a[1][0]); (c) String s = null; System.out.println(s.length()); (d) int[] a = new int[3]; System.out.println(a.length());
items.key: (a) ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; (b) prints 7; (c) NullPointerException; (d) does not compile
items.notes: (a): row 1 has length 1. (b): after a[0] = a[1], both slots refer to the same row. (d): length is a field on arrays, so it takes no parentheses; String has the length() method. All four were checked with javac/java.

items.prompt: Write pascal(n), which returns the first n rows of Pascal's triangle as a jagged array: row i has length i + 1, starts and ends with 1, and each inner entry is the sum of the two entries above it. pascal(4) is {{1}, {1, 1}, {1, 2, 1}, {1, 3, 3, 1}}, and pascal(0) is an array with no rows. Assume n >= 0.
items.notes: new int[n][n] gives rows of the wrong length (not jagged): take off points. Forgetting to allocate each row (new int[n][] with no tri[i] = new int[i + 1]) causes a NullPointerException.
